WildObs data follow the [Camera Trap Data Package](https://camtrap-dp.tdwg.org/) standard
(Camtrap DP), so they work with the growing set of tools built for it. This vignette takes
one WildObs project to three of them: the [camtrapdp](https://inbo.github.io/camtrapdp/) R
package, a [GBIF](https://www.gbif.org) Darwin Core export, and the
[camtrapR](https://jniedballa.github.io/camtrapR/) package, including its interactive
survey dashboard.

WildObs packages carry a few additions to the standard (see *Inside a WildObs data
package*). Most tools ignore what they do not know, but some check the standard strictly.
`as_camtrapdp()` removes the additions, reports every change it made, and checks the
result, so the package is canonical Camtrap DP.


``` r
library(WildObsR)

# your personal API key, read from .Renviron (see the Get started vignette)
api_key <- Sys.getenv("WILDOBSR_API_KEY")

# a small teaching survey at Dwyers Scrub, Queensland, with its media table, which Camtrap DP requires
id <- "QLD_Dwyers_Scrub_ANIM3018_2023_WildObsID_0005"
dp <- wildobs_dp_download(api_key = api_key, project_ids = id, media = TRUE)[[1]]
```

## Convert to canonical Camtrap DP


``` r
# remove the WildObs additions and check the result
out <- as_camtrapdp(dp, warn = "none")

# what was changed: how many fields, values and tables, by the kind of change
as.data.frame(table(where = out$report$level, change = out$report$action), responseName = "n") |>
  subset(n > 0)
#>       where                       change  n
#> 1     field                      dropped 10
#> 2   package                      dropped  7
#> 3  resource                      dropped  1
#> 8     value moved to vernacularNames$eng  1
#> 12    value       recoded RAiD -> Handle  1
#> 14  package                    repointed  1
#> 19 resource             schema repointed  3

# the converted package passes the Camtrap DP profile and the camtrapdp package's checks
c(profile = out$validation$descriptor$valid, camtrapdp = out$validation$camtrapdp$valid)
#>   profile camtrapdp 
#>      TRUE      TRUE
```

`out$report` lists every change, one row per field or value, with where it came from. The
`covariates` table is removed by default, because Camtrap DP has no place for it; use
`keep_covariates = TRUE` to keep it as an extra table, which the standard allows.

## Use it with camtrapdp, and export to GBIF

`out$camtrapdp` is already a `camtrapdp` object, so every camtrapdp function accepts it. For
example, its taxonomy, and a Darwin Core Archive ready to publish on GBIF:


``` r
# the taxa, in camtrapdp's own format
head(camtrapdp::taxa(out$camtrapdp)[, c("scientificName", "taxonRank")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   scientificName   taxonRank
#>   <chr>            <chr>    
#> 1 Alectura         genus    
#> 2 Alectura lathami species  
#> 3 Animal           phylum   
#> 4 Antechinus       genus    
#> 5 Aves             class    
#> 6 Blank            <NA>

# write the Darwin Core files GBIF reads
dwc_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "dwc")
suppressMessages(camtrapdp::write_dwc(out$camtrapdp, dwc_dir))
list.files(dwc_dir)
#> [1] "meta.xml"       "multimedia.csv" "occurrence.csv"
```

## Use it with camtrapR

camtrapR reads Camtrap DP from disk. Write the converted package, then read it back with
`camtrapR::readcamtrapDP()`, which returns camtrapR's camera table (one row per station) and
record table (one row per detection):


``` r
# save the converted package as CSV files and a datapackage.json
pkg_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "dwyers_scrub_camtrapdp")
frictionless::write_package(out$package, pkg_dir)

# read it the way camtrapR does
ct <- camtrapR::readcamtrapDP(
  deployments_file = file.path(pkg_dir, "deployments.csv"),
  media_file = file.path(pkg_dir, "media.csv"),
  observations_file = file.path(pkg_dir, "observations.csv"),
  datapackage_file = file.path(pkg_dir, "datapackage.json")
)

# stations, and detection records
dim(ct$CTtable)
#> [1] 32 27
dim(ct$recordTable)
#> [1] 2885   30
```

camtrapR joins every deployment at a station into one row and records the gaps between them
as `Problem` periods, so its camera operation matrix counts only the days a camera was
running. A station with a single deployment has no gaps, so camtrapR adds no `Problem`
columns; tell it whether there are any. From there, camtrapR builds detection histories
with effort:


``` r
# whether any station has gaps between its deployments
has_gaps <- any(grepl("^Problem", names(ct$CTtable)))

# days each station was operating
camop <- camtrapR::cameraOperation(CTtable = ct$CTtable, stationCol = "Station",
                                   setupCol = "Setup_date", retrievalCol = "Retrieval_date",
                                   hasProblems = has_gaps, dateFormat = "ymd HMS",
                                   writecsv = FALSE)

# animal detections that can be placed on a station
rec <- ct$recordTable[ct$recordTable$observationType == "animal" &
                        !grepl("^obscured_for_", ct$recordTable$deploymentID), ]
rec$Station <- rec$locationID

# weekly detection history of Australian brush-turkeys, with the camera-days behind each cell
dh <- camtrapR::detectionHistory(recordTable = rec, camOp = camop, stationCol = "Station",
                                 speciesCol = "scientificName",
                                 recordDateTimeCol = "DateTimeOriginal",
                                 recordDateTimeFormat = "ymd HMS", species = "Alectura lathami",
                                 occasionLength = 7, day1 = "station", includeEffort = TRUE,
                                 scaleEffort = FALSE, timeZone = "UTC")
# the first five stations, every week
head(dh$detection_history, 5)
#>                             o1 o2 o3
#> T1_C1_SEVT_WildObsID_0005    1  1  0
#> T1_C1_Sclero_WildObsID_0005  1  1  0
#> T1_C2_SEVT_WildObsID_0005    1  1  0
#> T1_C2_Sclero_WildObsID_0005  1  1  0
#> T1_C3_SEVT_WildObsID_0005    1  1  1
```

camtrapR reads the date-times as UTC, the time zone they are written in. Pass the project's
own time zone (`dp$temporal$timeZone`) where camtrapR asks for one if daily boundaries or
activity times matter.

## Explore it in the camtrapR survey dashboard

`camtrapR::surveyDashboard()` opens an interactive app for exploring and analysing a survey:
summaries, maps, activity patterns, species accumulation, and occupancy models. Pass it the
two tables read above:


``` r
camtrapR::surveyDashboard(
  CTtable = ct$CTtable, recordTable = rec,
  stationCol = "Station", setupCol = "Setup_date", retrievalCol = "Retrieval_date",
  hasProblems = has_gaps, CTdateFormat = "ymd HMS",
  xcol = "longitude", ycol = "latitude", crs = "epsg:4326",
  speciesCol = "scientificName", recordDateTimeCol = "DateTimeOriginal",
  recordDateTimeFormat = "ymd HMS", timeZone = "Australia/Brisbane"
)
```
